title: Challenges for journalism facing social networks, fake news and the distrust of z generation (Retos del periodismo frente a las redes sociales, las fake news y la desconfianza de la generacion Z)
screen_reason: Cross-sectional questionnaire of 465 Spanish 18-24 year-olds (Generation Z) on media use and fake news. Section 4.2 reports self-reported frequency of RECEIVING fake news with the full sample as denominator - 62.2% 'sometimes', 35.7% 'frequently or always', and in the conclusions '97% say they receive them' - which is a RECALL (self-reported exposure) share. Everything else in the paper is trust, self-perceived discernment, or perceived attribution of fake news to particular media/topics.

estimates.country: Spain (respondents drawn from several Autonomous Communities)
estimates.platform: Self-report questionnaire (no platform specified for the reception item)
estimates.date: Not stated; questionnaire administered after the onset of the COVID-19 crisis, article received 31/03/2021
estimates.measure_type: % of young Spaniards (18-24) who say they receive fake news at all (any frequency)
estimates.value_raw: el 97% de ellos afirma que las recibe (consistent with 62.2% 'a veces' + 35.7% 'con frecuencia o siempre' = 97.9%)
estimates.denominator: 465 Spanish university students aged 18-24 in Communication and Education degrees (convenience + snowball online sample)
estimates.definition: Respondent reporting any non-zero frequency of receiving fake news on the item 'Recepcion fake' (5-point Likert from 'nada o nunca' to 'mucho o todo')
estimates.misinfo_def: "fake news, informaciones falsas que, con apariencia de noticias periodisticas, se difunden deliberadamente para promover intereses particulares y que inducen a error a los lectores (Aruguete et al., 2020)" [EN: fake news, false information that, with the appearance of journalistic news, is deliberately spread to promote particular interests and that misleads readers]
estimates.source_quote: Respecto a las noticias falsas, declaran distinguirlas sólo la mitad de los encuestados, aunque el 97% de ellos afirma que las recibe.
estimates.page_loc: Section 5, Discusión y conclusiones, p. 80 (value); Section 4.2, p. 77 (underlying frequencies)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure self-report; respondents applied their own understanding of 'fake news' - the questionnaire text is not reproduced and no definition was shown to respondents as far as the paper reports. Instrument adapted from Media Use in the European Union (EC 2019) and Digital News Report.es 2020, validated by a 5-expert panel; Cronbach's alpha 0.79 and 0.82 across the two constructs.
estimates.moderator_quote: La muestra la forman 465 estudiantes en grados universitarios de Comunicación y Educación, todos comprendidos entre 18 y 24 años, es decir, pertenecientes a la llamada Generación Z (M= 21,5 DT=0.907; Min.=18; Máx.=25). [EN: The sample is made up of 465 undergraduate students in Communication and Education degrees, all aged between 18 and 24, i.e. belonging to the so-called Generation Z]
estimates.notes: EN translation of the source quote: 'Regarding fake news, only half of respondents say they can tell them apart, although 97% of them state that they receive them.' The 97% is stated verbatim by the authors in the conclusions; it is the authors' own rounding of the results-section frequencies (62.2% 'a veces' + 35.7% 'con frecuencia o siempre' = 97.9%), which is why I recorded 97 rather than 97.9. year=2021 is the publication/submission year: the paper never states when fieldwork took place (only that it followed the onset of the COVID-19 crisis; the article was received 31/03/2021). confidence=medium: non-probabilistic convenience+snowball sample of Communication and Education students, which the authors themselves flag as non-representative, and the paper contains several internal reporting inconsistencies (see rob).

estimates.notes: EN translation of the source quote: '62.2% state that they receive this type of content only sometimes, 35.7% state that they receive it frequently or always, so it is also explicit that practically the whole sample receives fake news.' definition_variant=true: this is the strict-threshold reading (frequently/always) of the same reception item as the 97%-any row above, same country x platform cell. The remaining 62.2% ('only sometimes') is the middle category and is not itself a threshold share, so it is not a third row. confidence=high on the number itself (verbatim, with the full sample as denominator); the sample's non-representativeness is captured in rob rather than in this field.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) MAIN JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator - the perceived-source items (Tabla 4, 'medios que crees que difunden más fake news', % answering 'Bastante' or 'Siempre', n = 465 each): word of mouth 76.5%, WhatsApp 74.1%, Facebook 69.4%, Twitter 66.6%, web pages 63.7%, Instagram 60.2%, TikTok 50.5%, traditional media 25%. These are perceptions of how much fake news each CHANNEL spreads, not the respondent's own encounter rate (a respondent who never uses TikTok can still rate TikTok high), so I read them as attribution-of-blame across media rather than 'perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment', and did not create eight RECALL rows that would dominate this paper's contribution to a prevalence distribution (R4). An adjudicator applying the 'perceived amount' clause more broadly could add them as RECALL/perceived rows with platform_norm set per channel; all values are recorded here. (2) Same call for Gráfico 5, perceived fake-news-prone CONTENT areas ('Bastante o Siempre'): politics 77.8%, humour and gossip 62.1%, health and diet 34.7%, sport 14.2%, entertainment 11%, academic 9.7%, fashion 7.3%, technology and video games 6.2%. Topic-level perception, same reasoning. (3) Self-perceived ability to DISTINGUISH fake news (41.7% only sometimes, 45.8% frequently, 11.4% always) is discernment/self-efficacy, explicitly excluded by the protocol. (4) Fact-checker awareness and use (61.1% do not know what they are, 38.7% do; among them 10% used Maldita.es, 6.7% Newtral, 1.5% Efe Verifica, 1.2% AFP Factual and Chequeado) is not misinformation exposure. (5) Trust/credibility items (77.8% little or no trust in politicians, 57.9% in social networks, 46.2% in media, 40.5% in journalists; 62.7% trust scientists) are not misinformation prevalence. (6) Media-consumption and platform-use frequencies (79% get informed via social networks 'frequently/always'; WhatsApp 81.8%, Instagram 74.8%, YouTube 51.1%, Twitter 38.5%) carry no veracity component. (7) Figures the paper cites from elsewhere are excluded per R8: Eurobarometer concern about disinformation (Spain 86%, Europe 74%), distrust of social networks (Spain 73%, Europe 65%), and Digital News Report shares (38%/40% of 18-24s preferring social networks; trust in media 36%).

rob.design: Cross-sectional online questionnaire (Google Forms) of 465 Spanish university students in Communication and Education degrees, aged 18-24 (M = 21.5, SD = 0.907; 52.47% women, 47.52% men), recruited by non-probabilistic convenience sampling combined with snowball referral across several Autonomous Communities; no sampling frame, no response rate, and no fieldwork dates are reported. Instrument adapted from Media Use in the European Union (European Commission, 2019) and Digital News Report.es 2020, refined by a five-expert panel (120 items cut to 105, eight reworded), 5-point Likert scales; reliability reported as Cronbach's alpha 0.79 and 0.82 averaged over the variables of each construct. Descriptive/exploratory analysis in SPSS, explicitly not inferential. The authors themselves state the key limitation: 'una de las limitaciones importantes del estudio es la falta de representatividad en la muestra' [EN: one of the study's important limitations is the lack of representativeness of the sample]. Additional caution: the paper is internally inconsistent in several places - the results say 'prácticamente el 100% de la muestra distingue las noticias falsas' while the conclusions say 'declaran distinguirlas sólo la mitad de los encuestados'; fact-checker awareness is 38.7% in the results but 'sólo el 40%' in the conclusions, and fact-checker use is itemised as 10%/6.7%/1.5%/1.2% but summarised as 'sólo el 19% había usado alguna vez uno'; the sample age is given as 18-24 but the descriptives report Max = 25. Only 'resultados parciales' of the wider project are presented.
rob.item6_quote: En este contexto de sobreabundancia informativa y de descentralización de la información es donde con mayor facilidad se distribuyen las denominadas fake news, informaciones falsas que, con apariencia de noticias periodísticas, se difunden deliberadamente para promover intereses particulares y que inducen a error a los lectores (Aruguete et al., 2020).
rob.item10_quote: El 62,2% declara que sólo recibe a veces este tipo de contenido, el 35,7% afirma que las recibe con frecuencia o siempre, de modo que también queda explícito que prácticamente la totalidad de la muestra recibe fake news.
